metadata.narrative: Our translational group is planning a small biomarker study alongside first-line immunotherapy for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma, but we are struggling to choose a focused biology panel rather than sequencing everything. Can you help me understand which HCC molecular subtypes and immune-microenvironment features we should prioritize? In particular, how should we think about TERT, TP53, CTNNB1/Wnt-beta-catenin, chromatin-remodeling mutations, VEGF/angiogenesis, and NASH-related disease when interpreting likely response or resistance to PD-1/PD-L1-based combinations? What should a pathologist, oncologist, and wet-lab team each keep in mind when translating this biology into a practical sample-annotation and assay plan?
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: A focused biomarker panel for a first-line immunotherapy HCC study should be built around a small number of recurrent driver alterations and a compact immune-microenvironment readout rather than broad sequencing.

Whole-exome data from The Cancer Genome Atlas established the core drivers to anchor any panel: TERT promoter mutations in roughly 44% of tumors, frequent TP53 mutation, CTNNB1 alterations in the Wnt pathway, and a subset (about 20%) with elevated immune-evasion gene expression that may mark immunotherapy-sensitive disease.

Gene-expression-based classification refines this further into five immune subtypes (C1–C5) in which TP53, CTNNB1, and AXIN1 mutation frequencies differ significantly, and the immune-enhanced C4 subtype shows the highest PD-1, PD-L1, and CTLA4 expression.

A complementary immunologic scheme separates tumors into an immune-active subtype enriched for interferon signaling and the T-cell chemoattractants CXCL9/CXCL10 versus an immune-exhausted subtype with high TGF-beta, while a distinct G4 molecular subclass lacks TP53/CTNNB1 mutations altogether and is instead driven by JAK/STAT/IL-6 signaling with brisk immune infiltration.

TERT promoter hotspot mutations (C228T/C250T) occur in about 47% of HCC and often arise as an early, second event following activation of Wnt signaling, so TERT is best used as a clonality/tumor-initiation marker rather than an immune-response predictor in its own right.

TP53's relationship to antitumor immunity is not uniform across cancers but is driven by the joint effects of tumor mutation burden and tumor aneuploidy level that a TP53 mutation induces, and experimentally restoring p53 expression reprograms the immune tumor microenvironment and can synergize with checkpoint blockade.
For panel design this argues for pairing TP53 status with a TMB/aneuploidy estimate rather than treating TP53 mutation as a standalone biomarker.

CTNNB1/Wnt-beta-catenin activation is the single most actionable resistance signal: CTNNB1 mutation suppresses the chemokine CCL19, paradoxically increasing correlation with PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint expression and CD8 T cells while producing an "immune-cold" phenotype that helps explain resistance to anti-PD-1/PD-L1 therapy.

Consistent with this, an immune-cell-infiltration (ICI) score analysis found that high-ICI tumors enriched for Wnt/beta-catenin activity and elevated checkpoint genes nonetheless had worse outcomes, and CTNNB1 mutation status significantly affected both ICI score and tumor mutation burden, supporting its use as a resistance biomarker.
CTNNB1 mutation frequency is also etiology-dependent, occurring in roughly a third of HCV-related HCC, which is relevant when annotating samples by underlying liver disease.

Chromatin-remodeling genes—ARID1A, ARID2, KMT2A, and MLL3—are frequently mutated in HCC, though how to therapeutically target these lesions remains undefined, and ARID2 inactivating mutations specifically occur in about 18% of HCV-associated HCC, again tying chromatin biology to viral etiology.

On the angiogenesis axis, HCC is a highly vascularized tumor dependent on VEGF, VEGF overexpression is more common in HCV- than HBV-related disease, and higher VEGF levels after locoregional therapy correlate with worse prognosis, framing VEGF as both a growth driver and a prognostic covariate.

Mechanistically, anti-VEGF therapy such as bevacizumab may act beyond simple angiogenesis blockade by targeting myeloid-derived suppressor cells, which is the immunologic rationale underlying atezolizumab-bevacizumab and newer durvalumab-bevacizumab-TACE combinations.

Baseline liver function, captured by ALBI grade or Child-Pugh class, meaningfully stratifies atezolizumab-bevacizumab efficacy and safety in post-hoc IMbrave150 analysis, so liver-function annotation belongs alongside any tumor biomarker.

NASH-related HCC deserves its own arm of interpretation: in a NASH mouse model, tumor-specific CD8 T cells expand peripherally but fail to control HCC growth because of higher intratumoral PD-1 expression, and depleting these exhausted cells with an anti-CD122 antibody restores tumor control.

Corroborating human data indicate that non-viral HCC, including NASH-driven disease, is less responsive to immunotherapy, with CD8+PD1+ T cells showing high TOX expression that impairs PD-1 degradation and blunts immune surveillance—an etiology effect that should be explicitly annotated rather than assumed away.

Broader immune-microenvironment features worth capturing include TGF-beta-driven Treg polarization and CD8 exhaustion, defective tumor antigen presentation, and the named HCC-associated antigens AFP, glypican-3, NY-ESO-1, MAGE-A, and hTERT that could inform future antigen-directed assays.

Single-cell spatial data show that checkpoint-blockade-driven CD8 reactivation requires physical proximity to dendritic cells and CD4 helper T cells, arguing for a spatial or multiplex readout rather than bulk expression alone.

At the trial level, high PD-L1 expression is associated with poor overall survival and the "cold" hepatobiliary microenvironment explains generally modest single-agent ICI benefit, motivating ongoing trials pairing immunotherapy with ablative techniques.

In CheckMate 040, PD-L1 positivity (≥1%) and a four-gene inflammatory signature were each significantly associated with improved overall survival and response to nivolumab, giving a concrete, tractable RNA/IHC starting panel.

The HIMALAYA trial's STRIDE regimen (single-priming tremelimumab plus durvalumab) improved OS over sorafenib while excluding patients with HBV/HCV coinfection or main portal vein thrombosis, details that matter for annotating trial-eligible biology.

For the pathologist, the practical task is standardizing preanalytics—consistent fixation, 3–5 µm section thickness, and a deliberate choice between chromogenic IHC and multiplex immunofluorescence—since these variables directly affect PD-L1 and other biomarker readouts.

Pathologists should also annotate each sample with etiology (viral, alcohol, NASH), BCLC stage, and Child-Pugh/ALBI grade at the time of biopsy or resection so molecular findings can be interpreted against liver-function and disease-etiology context.

For the oncologist, baseline and on-treatment AFP kinetics (a ≥15% decline by three months) and Child-Pugh/MELD-Na status are practical, low-cost biomarkers that track with survival and should be captured alongside tissue-based markers.
Oncologists should also flag NASH/non-viral etiology and CTNNB1/Wnt pathway status explicitly in case report forms, since both plausibly predict blunted response to PD-1/PD-L1-based combinations.

For the wet-lab team, a focused DNA panel covering the TERT promoter, TP53, CTNNB1/AXIN1, and the chromatin remodelers ARID1A/ARID2/KMT2A/MLL3, paired with an RNA/IHC module for PD-L1, CD8, CXCL9/10, TGF-beta, and a TMB estimate, captures most of the actionable biology without full sequencing.

Where budget allows, adding a spatial or multiplex assay to assess CD8–dendritic-cell–CD4 niches, plus a small panel of HCC tumor antigens (AFP, GPC3, NY-ESO-1, MAGE-A, hTERT), would future-proof the sample set for mechanistic follow-up.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

answer.text: A focused biomarker panel for a first-line immunotherapy HCC study should be built around a small number of recurrent driver alterations and a compact immune-microenvironment readout rather than broad sequencing.

Whole-exome data from The Cancer Genome Atlas established the core drivers to anchor any panel: TERT promoter mutations in roughly 44% of tumors, frequent TP53 mutation, CTNNB1 alterations in the Wnt pathway, and a subset (about 20%) with elevated immune-evasion gene expression that may mark immunotherapy-sensitive disease.

Gene-expression-based classification refines this further into five immune subtypes (C1–C5) in which TP53, CTNNB1, and AXIN1 mutation frequencies differ significantly, and the immune-enhanced C4 subtype shows the highest PD-1, PD-L1, and CTLA4 expression.

A complementary immunologic scheme separates tumors into an immune-active subtype enriched for interferon signaling and the T-cell chemoattractants CXCL9/CXCL10 versus an immune-exhausted subtype with high TGF-beta, while a distinct G4 molecular subclass lacks TP53/CTNNB1 mutations altogether and is instead driven by JAK/STAT/IL-6 signaling with brisk immune infiltration.

TERT promoter hotspot mutations (C228T/C250T) occur in about 47% of HCC and often arise as an early, second event following activation of Wnt signaling, so TERT is best used as a clonality/tumor-initiation marker rather than an immune-response predictor in its own right.

TP53's relationship to antitumor immunity is not uniform across cancers but is driven by the joint effects of tumor mutation burden and tumor aneuploidy level that a TP53 mutation induces, and experimentally restoring p53 expression reprograms the immune tumor microenvironment and can synergize with checkpoint blockade.
For panel design this argues for pairing TP53 status with a TMB/aneuploidy estimate rather than treating TP53 mutation as a standalone biomarker.

CTNNB1/Wnt-beta-catenin activation is the single most actionable resistance signal: CTNNB1 mutation suppresses the chemokine CCL19, paradoxically increasing correlation with PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint expression and CD8 T cells while producing an "immune-cold" phenotype that helps explain resistance to anti-PD-1/PD-L1 therapy.

Consistent with this, an immune-cell-infiltration (ICI) score analysis found that high-ICI tumors enriched for Wnt/beta-catenin activity and elevated checkpoint genes nonetheless had worse outcomes, and CTNNB1 mutation status significantly affected both ICI score and tumor mutation burden, supporting its use as a resistance biomarker.
CTNNB1 mutation frequency is also etiology-dependent, occurring in roughly a third of HCV-related HCC, which is relevant when annotating samples by underlying liver disease.

Chromatin-remodeling genes—ARID1A, ARID2, KMT2A, and MLL3—are frequently mutated in HCC, though how to therapeutically target these lesions remains undefined, and ARID2 inactivating mutations specifically occur in about 18% of HCV-associated HCC, again tying chromatin biology to viral etiology.

On the angiogenesis axis, HCC is a highly vascularized tumor dependent on VEGF, VEGF overexpression is more common in HCV- than HBV-related disease, and higher VEGF levels after locoregional therapy correlate with worse prognosis, framing VEGF as both a growth driver and a prognostic covariate.

Mechanistically, anti-VEGF therapy such as bevacizumab may act beyond simple angiogenesis blockade by targeting myeloid-derived suppressor cells, which is the immunologic rationale underlying atezolizumab-bevacizumab and newer durvalumab-bevacizumab-TACE combinations.

Baseline liver function, captured by ALBI grade or Child-Pugh class, meaningfully stratifies atezolizumab-bevacizumab efficacy and safety in post-hoc IMbrave150 analysis, so liver-function annotation belongs alongside any tumor biomarker.

NASH-related HCC deserves its own arm of interpretation: in a NASH mouse model, tumor-specific CD8 T cells expand peripherally but fail to control HCC growth because of higher intratumoral PD-1 expression, and depleting these exhausted cells with an anti-CD122 antibody restores tumor control.

Corroborating human data indicate that non-viral HCC, including NASH-driven disease, is less responsive to immunotherapy, with CD8+PD1+ T cells showing high TOX expression that impairs PD-1 degradation and blunts immune surveillance—an etiology effect that should be explicitly annotated rather than assumed away.

Broader immune-microenvironment features worth capturing include TGF-beta-driven Treg polarization and CD8 exhaustion, defective tumor antigen presentation, and the named HCC-associated antigens AFP, glypican-3, NY-ESO-1, MAGE-A, and hTERT that could inform future antigen-directed assays.

Single-cell spatial data show that checkpoint-blockade-driven CD8 reactivation requires physical proximity to dendritic cells and CD4 helper T cells, arguing for a spatial or multiplex readout rather than bulk expression alone.

At the trial level, high PD-L1 expression is associated with poor overall survival and the "cold" hepatobiliary microenvironment explains generally modest single-agent ICI benefit, motivating ongoing trials pairing immunotherapy with ablative techniques.

In CheckMate 040, PD-L1 positivity (≥1%) and a four-gene inflammatory signature were each significantly associated with improved overall survival and response to nivolumab, giving a concrete, tractable RNA/IHC starting panel.

The HIMALAYA trial's STRIDE regimen (single-priming tremelimumab plus durvalumab) improved OS over sorafenib while excluding patients with HBV/HCV coinfection or main portal vein thrombosis, details that matter for annotating trial-eligible biology.

For the pathologist, the practical task is standardizing preanalytics—consistent fixation, 3–5 µm section thickness, and a deliberate choice between chromogenic IHC and multiplex immunofluorescence—since these variables directly affect PD-L1 and other biomarker readouts.

Pathologists should also annotate each sample with etiology (viral, alcohol, NASH), BCLC stage, and Child-Pugh/ALBI grade at the time of biopsy or resection so molecular findings can be interpreted against liver-function and disease-etiology context.

For the oncologist, baseline and on-treatment AFP kinetics (a ≥15% decline by three months) and Child-Pugh/MELD-Na status are practical, low-cost biomarkers that track with survival and should be captured alongside tissue-based markers.
Oncologists should also flag NASH/non-viral etiology and CTNNB1/Wnt pathway status explicitly in case report forms, since both plausibly predict blunted response to PD-1/PD-L1-based combinations.

For the wet-lab team, a focused DNA panel covering the TERT promoter, TP53, CTNNB1/AXIN1, and the chromatin remodelers ARID1A/ARID2/KMT2A/MLL3, paired with an RNA/IHC module for PD-L1, CD8, CXCL9/10, TGF-beta, and a TMB estimate, captures most of the actionable biology without full sequencing.

Where budget allows, adding a spatial or multiplex assay to assess CD8–dendritic-cell–CD4 niches, plus a small panel of HCC tumor antigens (AFP, GPC3, NY-ESO-1, MAGE-A, hTERT), would future-proof the sample set for mechanistic follow-up.
